title: 7 Best Ceiling Paints in 2026: Flat Finishes That Hide Flaws
metaDescription: Benjamin Moore Waterborne Ceiling Paint (508) is the best ceiling paint for most rooms thanks to its ultra-flat finish. Seven picks by room and budget.

intro:
The best ceiling paint for most rooms is Benjamin Moore Waterborne Ceiling Paint (508). Its ultra-flat finish hides roller laps and drywall seams in side light, it is formulated to resist spatter, and its longer open time makes it easier to keep a wet edge across a big ceiling.

The right pick still changes with the ceiling and the room. Patched plaster wants a high-hide paint like Sherwin-Williams Eminence, steamy bathrooms and kitchens want a mildew-resistant formula, and new drywall needs a primer before any finish coat. Below are seven picks, then answers to the questions people ask before painting: which sheen, how much paint, and how to avoid roller marks.
quickAnswer: Buy Benjamin Moore Waterborne Ceiling Paint (508) for living rooms and any ceiling that catches side light. Choose Sherwin-Williams Eminence for patched or uneven ceilings, BEHR Premium Plus for budget whole-house repaints, KILZ Color Change if you struggle to see coverage, and Zinsser Perma-White for bathrooms and high-humidity kitchens. Prime new drywall with a PVA primer and plan on two coats.

sections.heading: The 7 Best Ceiling Paints in 2026, Ranked
sections.body:
These paints and primers are ranked from manufacturer data sheets and labels: sheen, spatter and dry-time claims, coverage, stain-blocking and mildew features, warranty terms and consistent owner feedback. No room trials were run; label claims are described as such.

### Best Overall: Benjamin Moore Waterborne Ceiling Paint (508)

Benjamin Moore's Waterborne Ceiling Paint, product 508, is the paint professional painters reach for when a ceiling has to disappear. Its ultra-flat finish carries essentially no sheen, so low-angle light from windows and wall sconces does not pick out roller laps, patches or taped drywall seams the way a slightly shinier paint would.

Benjamin Moore formulates it to resist spatter, which matters when you are rolling straight overhead, and it stays workable longer than many ceiling paints. That extra open time lets you blend each roller section into the last before it starts to set, the key to a ceiling without lap lines. It can be tinted to pale colors if you want a ceiling a shade warmer or cooler than stark white, and it is low odor. The downsides are cost and availability: it sells through Benjamin Moore dealers and costs more than big-box paints. For living rooms, kitchens and any space where the ceiling catches strong side light, owners and pros rate it consistently high.

**Pros:** Ultra-flat finish hides laps and seams; formulated to resist spatter; longer open time; tintable; low odor.

**Cons:** Costs more than big-box ceiling paints; sold mainly through dealers.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Benjamin+Moore+Waterborne+Ceiling+Paint+508&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best for Imperfect Ceilings: Sherwin-Williams Eminence

Eminence High Performance Ceiling Paint is Sherwin-Williams' premium ceiling product, and hiding flaws is what it does best. The finish is very flat and the body is thick and high-hiding, so it masks patched spots, small texture variations and the ghosts of old repairs better than most.

Sherwin-Williams markets it for low spatter and, in many cases, one-coat coverage over a similar color, and some versions add stain-blocking properties for minor marks. It suits older homes with plaster ceilings patched over the decades, rooms with a lot of raking light, and anyone who would rather skip a second coat. It is expensive at full price, and the heavy body takes some getting used to on the roller, especially when cutting in. Sherwin-Williams runs regular sales, and timing a purchase to one makes a real difference. Owners most often cite its hiding power as the reason they chose it.

**Pros:** Very flat, high-hide finish; low spatter; often one coat over a similar color; some versions block minor stains.

**Cons:** Expensive at full price; thick body feels heavy on the roller.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Sherwin-Williams+Eminence+ceiling+paint&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Value: BEHR Premium Plus Ceiling Paint

BEHR Premium Plus Ceiling Paint is the sensible pick when every ceiling in the house needs paint. It is a flat interior ceiling paint that hides minor flaws well, it is stocked at Home Depot, and the store can tint it to light ceiling colors. Across several rooms, the savings over a premium dealer brand add up quickly.

The compromises are typical of value ceiling paints. It may need two coats over stains, patches or a darker previous color, and it spatters more than premium formulas, so drop cloths and safety glasses are worth the bother. Like any ceiling paint, it will not seal a water stain on its own, so spot-prime those first. For bedrooms, hallways, closets and general repaints over ceilings in decent shape, owners generally find it does the job well.

**Pros:** Name-brand flat ceiling paint at a lower cost; hides minor flaws; easy to find; low odor and water cleanup; tintable.

**Cons:** May need two coats over stains or darker colors; more spatter than premium paints.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=BEHR+Premium+Plus+ceiling+paint&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best for Beginners: KILZ Color Change Ceiling Paint

The hardest part of repainting a white ceiling white is seeing where you have already rolled. KILZ Color Change Ceiling Paint solves that by going on with a visible tint and drying to white, so each pass is easy to track while wet.

Missed spots, thin areas and uneven overlaps stand out before the paint dries, which helps beginners lay an even coat and lets experienced painters move faster. Once dry it is a flat white that hides minor flaws. Because the color shift depends on drying, it can lag in cool or humid rooms, so wait for the full change before judging coverage. It is designed to dry white, so tint options are limited. For anyone repainting white over white, especially in large or bright rooms, owners keep mentioning how much easier it makes judging coverage.

**Pros:** Goes on tinted and dries white so you see coverage; makes missed spots obvious; flat finish; good for first-timers.

**Cons:** Color change lags in cool or humid rooms; fewer tint and finish options.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=KILZ+Color+Change+ceiling+paint&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best for Bathrooms and Kitchens: Zinsser Perma-White

Bathroom ceilings take steam every day, and many grow mildew spots within a year of painting. Zinsser Perma-White Mold and Mildew-Proof Interior Paint is formulated with a mildewcide that resists growth on the paint film, and the label carries a mildew-resistance guarantee.

It is self-priming on many surfaces and dries to a scrubbable, moisture-resistant finish, which makes it a strong pick for bathrooms, laundry rooms, basements and kitchens where humidity is high. It comes in several sheens; satin or eggshell are common choices for bathroom ceilings because they wipe clean more easily than flat, though they show more imperfections. It does not fix the cause of mildew: without a working exhaust fan vented outside, moisture still condenses. Clean off existing mildew before painting.

**Pros:** Resists mold and mildew on the paint film; self-priming on many surfaces; scrubbable finish; several sheens.

**Cons:** Sheens are glossier than typical flat ceiling paint; does not solve poor ventilation.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Zinsser+Perma-White+mold+mildew+proof+interior+paint&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Budget: Glidden Interior Ceiling Paint

Glidden's ceiling paint is the least expensive option here and fills a practical niche: ceilings where budget matters more than appearance. It is a flat white interior paint that suits most ceilings, cleans up with water and is easy to find.

For closets, utility rooms, unfinished basements, garages and rental turnovers, it covers adequately at a cost that makes large areas affordable. The trade-offs are predictable. Coverage is thinner than premium paints, so plan on two coats in most cases, especially over patches or a dingy old ceiling, and expect more spatter. It will not hide flaws under raking light as well as an ultra-flat premium paint, and it does not block stains by itself. In a main living area with lots of light, spending more usually pays off.

**Pros:** Low cost per gallon; flat white finish; widely stocked; low odor and water cleanup.

**Cons:** Thinner coverage, usually two coats; more spatter than premium paints.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Glidden+interior+ceiling+paint&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Primer for New Drywall: KILZ PVA Drywall Primer

New drywall and joint compound absorb paint at different rates. If ceiling paint goes straight on, taped seams and patches often show as dull or shiny stripes, a defect called flashing. KILZ PVA Drywall Primer seals the surface so the topcoat lays down evenly.

PVA primers are inexpensive, roll easily and dry quickly, and this one is widely stocked. It is the right primer for new drywall ceilings, large patches and skim-coated areas. It is not a stain blocker, so water stains, smoke damage and nicotine need a shellac or oil-based stain-blocking primer instead. It is also not meant for previously painted ceilings, which usually need only cleaning. Use one coat on bare drywall, then two coats of ceiling paint.

**Pros:** Seals drywall and compound for even absorption; low cost; easy to roll; quick drying; reduces flashing.

**Cons:** Not a stain blocker; only for new or bare drywall.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=KILZ+PVA+drywall+primer&tag=sktiger-20)

sections.heading: Is Ceiling Paint Different From Wall Paint?
sections.body:
Yes. Ceiling paint is usually thicker, flatter and slower to set than wall paint, and each difference makes overhead work easier.

### Thicker, so it stays on the roller

A more viscous paint clings to the roller instead of dripping and flings fewer fine droplets as the roller turns. That keeps floors, furniture and your face cleaner.

### Flatter, so light does not catch it

Ceiling paints are almost always flat or ultra-flat. A ceiling is lit at a low angle by windows and lamps, which exaggerates any shine, so even a little sheen shows roller laps, patches and seams.

### More open time for a wet edge

Many ceiling paints stay workable longer. Open time is the window in which wet paint can still blend with the next section. Overhead work is slower than walls, so those extra minutes help.

### Can you swap them?

Flat wall paint will go on a ceiling, but you lose spatter control and some hiding. Flat ceiling paint on walls is fine in low-traffic rooms, but it is not made to be scrubbed and marks easily.

### What to look for on the can

Look for phrases like spatter-resistant, ultra-flat or dead-flat, and extended open time, plus a coverage figure and recoat time on the data sheet. A can that says only interior flat white is usually a general-purpose flat paint: it works, but it helps you less overhead.

sections.heading: What Sheen Should Ceiling Paint Be?
sections.body:
Flat or ultra-flat for nearly every ceiling, with matte, eggshell or satin reserved for bathrooms, kitchens and laundry rooms where you need to wipe the surface.

### Why side light exposes flaws

Daylight from a window strikes the ceiling at a shallow angle, so every bump, roller ridge and change in sheen throws a shadow or reflects differently. A patch invisible when you look straight up can stand out from across the room in late afternoon.

### How flat paint hides them

Ultra-flat paints carry very little sheen, so the whole ceiling reflects light the same way even where the film is thicker or a patch absorbed paint differently. That is why premium ceiling paints earn their cost in rooms with big windows or skylights.

### What about a shiny ceiling?

Some people search for the best paint for a shiny ceiling. A higher sheen does make a ceiling reflect more light, but it also magnifies every flaw, so it only works on a near-perfect, smooth surface. In most homes a flat white with a high light reflectance value brightens the room without the risk.

| Sheen | Hides flaws | Cleanability | Best ceiling use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ultra-flat | Excellent | Low | Living rooms, bedrooms, bright rooms |
| Flat | Very good | Low to moderate | Most rooms |
| Matte or eggshell | Good | Moderate | Kitchens, kids' rooms |
| Satin | Fair | Good | Bathrooms, laundry rooms |
| Semi-gloss | Poor | Very good | Rarely; humid utility spaces |

sections.heading: What Is the Best Ceiling Paint for Each Room?
sections.body:
Use an ultra-flat premium paint in bright living spaces, a good flat in bedrooms, a mildew-resistant paint in bathrooms and kitchens, and a primer first on new or stained ceilings.

### Living rooms

Living rooms get the most raking light, so they reward an ultra-flat premium paint such as Benjamin Moore 508 or Sherwin-Williams Eminence. Eminence is the better pick when the ceiling has old patches or uneven texture.

### Bedrooms and hallways

A good flat paint like BEHR Premium Plus usually does fine, especially on a ceiling in good shape. KILZ Color Change helps if you are repainting white over white and want to see your coverage.

### Kitchens

Kitchens see grease and steam. A matte or eggshell finish you can wipe down is the better choice, and Zinsser Perma-White adds mildew resistance. Degrease the ceiling before painting so the new coat bonds.

### Bathrooms and other high-humidity rooms

Use a mildew-resistant paint such as Zinsser Perma-White in satin or eggshell, and make sure the exhaust fan works and vents outside. If mildew is already present, clean it first; our [mold remover guide](/best-mold-remover/) explains which cleaner suits which surface.

### Basements, garages and porches

Budget paints such as Glidden are fine for basement and garage ceilings. The same spaces often benefit from a floor coating; see our [concrete floor paint picks](/best-concrete-floor-paint/). Porch ceilings and soffits need exterior paint, not interior ceiling paint.

sections.heading: How Do You Prep a Ceiling Before Painting?
sections.body:
Seal stains, repair cracks and nail pops, clean off grease and soap, and test older textured ceilings before you disturb them.

### Seal stains first

Ceiling paint will not hide water stains, smoke damage, nicotine or marker; they bleed through water-based paint, sometimes within hours. Fix the leak, let the drywall dry, then seal the stain with a shellac-based or oil-based stain-blocking primer. Ventilate well, since solvent primers smell far stronger than latex.

### Repair cracks and nail pops

Fill hairline cracks with lightweight spackle; cracks that keep returning at joints may need retaping. Reset nail pops or replace them with drywall screws and cover with compound. Sand smooth and spot-prime patches so they do not flash.

### Clean grease and soap

Residue stops paint from bonding, especially in kitchens and bathrooms. Wipe with a mild degreaser, rinse and let dry.

### Prime new drywall

Bare drywall and compound absorb paint unevenly, so seams flash through the topcoat. One coat of a PVA primer such as KILZ PVA, then two coats of ceiling paint.

### Test old textures and paint

Popcorn and acoustic textures applied before the 1980s may contain asbestos, and paint in homes built before 1978 may contain lead. Have a sample tested before scraping or sanding. Painting over intact texture is usually safer than removing it; use a thick-nap roller with light pressure, or spray it with a [paint sprayer](/best-paint-sprayer/) so the texture does not loosen.

sections.heading: How Do You Paint a Ceiling Without Roller Marks?
sections.body:
Cut in one wall at a time, roll small sections back into wet paint, never stop mid-ceiling, and apply two thin coats.

### Tools that help

Use an extension pole that reaches about 2 to 4 feet for standard 8- to 9-foot ceilings, a sturdy frame, and a quality woven or microfiber cover: 3/8 to 1/2 inch nap for smooth ceilings, 3/4 inch or more for heavy texture. Cheap covers shed fibers and spatter. Cut in with a 2 to 2.5 inch angled sash brush.

### Cut in one wall at a time

Brush a 2 to 3 inch band where ceiling meets wall, but only along one wall, then roll that area while the band is still wet. Cutting in the whole room first lets the band dry and leaves a picture-frame outline.

### Roll in 4-by-4-foot sections

Load the roller evenly and work in sections about 4 feet square. Start a few inches from the last wet edge and roll back into it, spreading paint in a W, then fill in with parallel strokes and finish with light passes in one direction.

### Keep a wet edge to the end

Work across the room's shorter dimension and finish each ceiling in one session. If you must stop, stop at a beam or corner.

### Second coat

Many painters lay final strokes parallel to the main window light. Wait the label recoat time, often a few hours, then roll the second coat perpendicular to the first. Never go back over paint that has started to set.

sections.heading: How Much Ceiling Paint Do You Need?
sections.body:
Most ceiling paints list about 350 to 400 square feet per gallon on smooth, primed surfaces, so one gallon usually covers a 12 by 14 foot bedroom ceiling in two coats. Textured ceilings and new drywall take more.

### Estimate the gallons

Multiply the room's length by its width. A 12 by 14 foot ceiling is 168 square feet; two coats is 336 square feet, about one gallon. A 20 by 20 foot living room is 400 square feet; two coats need about two to three gallons.

| Room | Ceiling area | Gallons for two coats |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Small bathroom | 50 sq ft | Under 1; a quart may do |
| Bedroom (12 x 14) | 168 sq ft | About 1 |
| Living room (20 x 20) | 400 sq ft | 2 to 3 |
| Whole 1,500 sq ft home | 1,500 sq ft | 8 to 9 |

### Allow for texture

Popcorn and heavy knockdown can take up to twice as much paint as a smooth ceiling. Buy extra rather than running short mid-ceiling.

### Box the cans

Buy all the paint at once and pour the cans together in a large bucket so color and sheen match across the ceiling. Label a small leftover with the room and date for touch-ups, which blend best from the same batch.

### Hiring it out

Painters commonly charge more per square foot for ceilings than for walls because of the setup and difficulty. Premium dealer brands such as Benjamin Moore and Sherwin-Williams are often discounted during their regular sales, so a whole-house job is worth timing. If you are renovating floors at the same time, paint the ceiling first, then install [vinyl plank flooring](/best-vinyl-plank-flooring/) or [laminate](/best-laminate-flooring/) so drips never reach the new floor.

mistakes.title: Painting over a water stain without sealing it
mistakes.body: Water stains bleed through ordinary ceiling paint, often within hours. Fix the leak, let the area dry and seal the stain with a shellac or oil-based stain-blocking primer first. A paint labeled stain-resistant may handle minor marks, but it does not replace primer on real water or smoke damage.

mistakes.title: Choosing a paint with too much sheen
mistakes.body: Even a slight sheen highlights roller marks, patches and seams once side light hits the ceiling. Most ceilings look best in flat or ultra-flat. Keep satin and eggshell for bathrooms and kitchens where you need to wipe the surface, and expect them to show more flaws.

mistakes.title: Cutting in the whole room before rolling
mistakes.body: If the brushed band along the walls dries before you roll next to it, the brushed and rolled areas look different and leave a frame around the ceiling. Cut in one wall at a time and roll that stretch while the band is still wet so the finish stays even to the edges.

mistakes.title: Stopping halfway across the ceiling
mistakes.body: A break mid-ceiling lets the wet edge dry, and a lap line appears where you restart. Plan to finish each ceiling in one session, and if you must stop, do it at a corner or beam. Rolling across the shorter dimension of the room makes the wet edge easier to keep.

mistakes.title: Skipping primer on new drywall
mistakes.body: Fresh drywall and joint compound soak up paint unevenly, so seams and patches flash through the finish. A PVA drywall primer seals the surface and lets ceiling paint go on evenly. Skip it and you often need extra finish coats, and the seams may still show in raking light.

faqs.q: What is the best ceiling paint?
faqs.a: Benjamin Moore Waterborne Ceiling Paint (508) is the best ceiling paint for most rooms. Its ultra-flat finish hides roller marks and seams in side light, it is formulated to resist spatter, and its longer open time helps you keep a wet edge. Sherwin-Williams Eminence is the better pick for patched or imperfect ceilings.

faqs.q: Who makes the best ceiling paint?
faqs.a: Benjamin Moore and Sherwin-Williams make the most highly rated ceiling paints for appearance, with the 508 Waterborne Ceiling Paint and Eminence. BEHR and Glidden lead on value, KILZ makes a useful color-change paint and the PVA primer for new drywall, and Zinsser leads for mildew-resistant paint in bathrooms.

faqs.q: What is the best ceiling paint for a bedroom or living room?
faqs.a: For a living room with big windows, use an ultra-flat premium paint such as Benjamin Moore 508 or Sherwin-Williams Eminence, because raking light shows every flaw in a lesser paint. For bedrooms with ceilings in good shape, a quality flat like BEHR Premium Plus usually looks just as good for less.

faqs.q: What is the best ceiling paint for a kitchen or high-humidity room?
faqs.a: A mildew-resistant paint such as Zinsser Perma-White in an eggshell or satin finish is the best choice for kitchens, bathrooms and laundry rooms. It resists mildew growth on the paint film and wipes clean. Degrease the ceiling first, and make sure an exhaust fan vents moisture outside.

faqs.q: Does a ceiling need two coats of paint?
faqs.a: Most ceilings look better with two coats, especially over new drywall, patches or a color change. A high-hide paint such as Sherwin-Williams Eminence over a similar white in good condition may cover in one. Two thin coats give a more even finish than one heavy coat and hide roller marks and flashing better.

faqs.q: Can you use wall paint on a ceiling?
faqs.a: Yes, a flat wall paint will work on a ceiling, but you give up the spatter resistance, extra hiding and longer open time that ceiling paint is formulated for. Ceiling-specific paint usually costs little more and makes overhead rolling cleaner and more even, so it is worth buying for any main room.

faqs.q: How do I paint a popcorn ceiling?
faqs.a: First, if the home was built before the 1980s, have the texture tested for asbestos. If it is safe and intact, roll it with a thick-nap cover using light pressure, or spray it, so the texture does not loosen. Avoid overworking any area, and buy extra paint because texture soaks up much more than smooth drywall.

bottomLine: Benjamin Moore Waterborne Ceiling Paint (508) is the best ceiling paint for most homes, because its ultra-flat, spatter-resistant finish makes a ceiling disappear in any light. Use Sherwin-Williams Eminence on patched or uneven ceilings, BEHR Premium Plus for budget whole-house repaints, KILZ Color Change if you want to see your coverage, Zinsser Perma-White in bathrooms and kitchens, Glidden for utility spaces and KILZ PVA primer under every new drywall ceiling. The can is only half the result: seal stains, prime new drywall, use a good roller cover, cut in one wall at a time and finish each ceiling in a single session.
